commentBody: Put up a bit of a challenge, which I like, plus solid long entries. Thanks!
Either I’ve been doing these puzzles too long, or that was an easier Friday.
Thanks for a fun puzzle and congrats on your NYT debut!

This was a fine Friday puzzle, more Fridaylike than at least three recent Fridays that felt more like Saturdays.

This was probably on the easy side even for a Friday, since a lot of the long answers were guessable with only a few letters. (E.g., EPISTOLARY NOVEL just from the clue, and PUTS ON A PEDESTAL just from the clue and the last three letters.) Which of course led to lots more letters from the crossings.

I think I didn't  understand the clue "High concept?" for CLOUD NINE. Sure, a cloud is high in the sky — is that it? I just know this phrase in the expression "on cloud nine" meaning very happy. Does that make it a "concept"? And is there some pun that occasions the "?" ?
i'd never heard of a molerat until i started watching kim possible.  that was in a prior life,it seems.  i suppose it's out of production now.
A thinly fictionalized life was written of Simon the Zealot.  It was the first APOSTOLARY NOVEL.

Loved this Friday! One of those puzzles where the constructor’s sense of humor and way with cultural references just clicked for me. Two minutes faster than my average, but didn’t feel like a breeze or a snooze, just a quick little pleasure, with any blindspots covered by well-thought-out crosses. I’ve been solving all the gimmicky Sundays and Thursdays from the archives, so I may have been biased toward what a straight shot this was. Either way, more please!
Loved this one! No complaints at all. Made me work hard enough to feel a sense of accomplishment!
Great puzzle.
Anyone know why Rocky solves to YOS
I just want to say that (with some look ups) I have just completed my very first EVER Friday crossword!
Epistolary novel — I just finished an extraordinary one: Pamela, by Samuel Richardson, 1740. Highly recommended.
It was pretty much self contained, without much trivia or pop culture. I foundered on kapow and allow.  I had allot and kapot, like a misspelling of kaput.
My late ‘90s /early 2000s of culture knowledge comes in handy at last. Thanks to 14a, this is my fastest ever Friday solve.

Lots of fresh cluing and fill. Perfect for a Friday. But the northwest corner was brutal and a bit Naticky for me- EPISTOLARY crossed with EPICINE crossed with what I assume are two US sports references (SHEA and ACC) almost did me in.
Good puzzle.  Muddled my way through, but I made it!
This was my fastest Friday ever, by far, yet it didnt seem out of place. I enjoyed it! Good puzzle!
This was my first gold star on a Friday!
Too fast for my liking but I enjoyed the long entries.

A Short Epistolary Novel

Rocky: Yo, Top Chef, should I put a skirt steak or strip steak on my black eye? Apollo Creed's sidearm went KAPOW and before you know it I was on the mat seeing glitter and they was giving me smelling salts...

Top Chef: Dear Rocky, I assume you are that All American Hero many people put on a pedestal without realizing you're just the star of a feelgood movie? My advice, cook the steak -- bone in -- in shea butter while baking an Idaho potato, until the steak looks sepia in color. Sincerely, TC

Rocky: Yo, Top Chef, the diets I'm on don't allow for no steak. I can eat tabouli, maybe some ravioli, and I've definitely ate crow. But steak makes me tired, and yo, a guy like me needs to stay erect.

Top Chef: My dear sir, I shall not stand for this filth! You are behaving like an absolute αss!

Rocky: Yo, Top Chef, I'm sorry. Oops, I did it again, mixed up the terms. I meant to say a guy like me needs to be standing up. I mean, last time I was in the ring, some epicene molerat named Rhoda fought me to a tie vote. Now Tyra Banks says I'm no longer gonna be America's Top Model and has refused to give me the keypad number to her door!

Top Chef: Yo, I'm sorry, for throwing a fit like a baby with colic. I have not a clue what to do for your eye. Do you have one of those medical kits that moms used to use?

Rocky: Yo, it was so easy, know what I did? Sat down, read Neruda's ode to Marti, before you know it I was on cloud nine!

[cue the cellos]

Pleasant, fizzy, easeny Friday with some fun fill.

And typically, too-easy latter-day cluing too often.  Grid-spanning fill like PUTSONAPEDESTAL should never be gimme or gimmee-adjacent.

I'd'a certainly clued "Rocky openings" without the "?" in a nod to late week.

Nice debut Adam! I thought it was an interesting grid too. and fun spanners.
 
Not so difficult overall but I had an awful lot of misdirects. TIEGAME before TIEVOTE, SPECIAL delivery before SIDEARM, SIMPLE before SOEASY, ACRE before DOOR (Ok that’s a lot of acres), BUILT before BASED, NOSES before SALTS. Not sure if all those were deliberate but they kept me on my toes in what otherwise was a fairly smooth solve. Friends overseas, SIDEARM is a pitcher’s delivery in baseball, not the weapon.

For another great EPISTOLARY NOVEL try Jane Austen’s “Lady Susan”. It was made into a fairly decent movie “Love and Friendship” with a nice role for Kate Beckinsale. Speaking of which is anyone else dreading the new “Sense and Sensibiltiy”? The Emma Thompson version was just so darned perfect I just can’t bear to watch anything lesser, and all the Gen Z intensity is just too much for Austen I think.

Anyway, I was looking for a medieval epic or fantasy at first for “mail centric”.

Loved the YOS for Rocky opening but wonder why they used him as the HERO since that made that a bit easier by putting it in my mind. Although maybe it would have been too opaque otherwise.

Shout out to RHODA and Valerie Harper, what a great show and actress.

Nothing else too noteworthy to me but definitely a solid grid all around especially for a debut. Glad you stuck with it!

@Sam please don't shorthand a school's sports conference to just "football". UVA has a rich history in the ACC in many more women's and men's sports. (Their football program isn't even all that great, historically)

I enjoyed most of this puzzle with its smart misdirection. The lower two thirds came together quite quickly but not at all easily. However, I needed several lookups in the top section (the Cuban, the spin-off show, the reality show), and the crossing of EPI__NE, AC_ and SH_A was an triple uber-natick for me.

Why are "Rocky openings" YOS?

Why do "Some deliveries" solve to SIDEARM?

I've made TABBOULI several times, but I've known it as "tabbouleh", and it's on the menu of out fave local Lebanese restaurant as "tabouli". Transliteration of such words is a fascinatingly complex thing, isn't it?

"Yo, Adrian, I did it!" - Me, phone raised in triumph, to the empty living room after finishing this puzzle. 

Nice debut! Crisp and clean Friday. Congrats to the new constructor.
Fun puzzle. Congratulations on your debut!

The world makes sense again.

I thought the puzzle was puzzling, whereas no small number have commented that they thought it rather easy.

The NE was a honey badger for me.  I didn't know the Cuban philosopher, and TIEgamE completely wrecked any progress there.  RAVIOLI made sense only in retrospect (I was thinking "hot" as in spicy hot).  And [Small sounds] was every bit a Friday clue, in my book.

Strange puzzle for me in that the longer answers were easier for me.  It was the shorter ones that got me.  [Riot] for instance.  Smelling SALTS came to me only after much consternation.

Really?  There's a EBOW?  Violinists have it SO EASY these days, I guess.  Are there EStrummers and EPickers for guitars?  And "E-key pushers" for pianos?  What does the musician actually do these days?

Anyway, while this was a great chewy and very jungly puzzle, it took me as long as in the days BCE (before crossword easening).
This puzzle is so BASED, as the kids would say, not meaning predicted...
DIOR wasnt one of 412 in the White House.  Thought it was for this White House!  Great debut!
YO, Adrian!!! I just learned that your name is EPICENE!

Hello, everyone.

I'm a mule rat, an apparently fictional but very reasonable sounding animal.

And I am quite disgruntled.

Just because I don't exist, that doesn't mean I shouldn't have my own entry in a crossword.  Things that actually exist are very discriminatory against those of us who don't.  And you wouldn't like it either if you didn't exist.  Whatever happened to "do unto other mule rats, as you would have them do unto you"?  Huh?  Huh? 

Imaginary creatures of the world unite.  We have nothing to lose.  (Duh--we don't exist to have anything).

Excuse me while I go back (in my imagination) to my mule rat house and eat some mule rat food and plan some mule rat revenge.  

Mule be sorry you didn't acknowledge us.

🫏🐀

Congratulations on your NYT debut, Adam! Maybe I'm just TIRED, but it's the first NYT Friday puzzle in a long while that I wondered if I would be able to finish. 

I'd only known of José Martí from his efforts to liberate Cuba from Spain, so I was reluctant to put that answer in. The whole of the first three or four rows really gave me trouble. 

I'm encouraged by your 100+ iterations of this grid. It's been a while since I've tried to construct a puzzle, but maybe I just need to put in a little more time to get a grid I'm happy with.

Hope we'll see you back here again.
The singular of phalanges is phalanx. There is no such thing as a "phalange."

A sorta easy and sorta tough one… I waltzed through everything until I stared for what seemed a lifetime at the epistolary clue. Also had never heard of Yenta. 
Good Friday 👏
If I have ever seen the words EPICENE or EPISTOLARY, I do not recall it.  That still did not stop me from completing this puzzle in 25% less time than average.  Happy Friday!
Congrats on the great debut!

The singular of “phalanges” is phalanx, not phalange. 

I just out-nerded you!
I've got that song stuck in my head now: "Oops, I wrote another epistolary novel". Britney may be an all-American hero, but I've got to stop putting her on a pedestal and go to bed.
Tough for a Friday. Grid wasn't wanting to give anything up as a gimme, except 14A.

Most of the time the celli (cellos) are on the right of the stage here at the Seattle symphony. In fact, it is a prerogative of the conductor where she/he wants the various sections of the orchestra positioned.

Ebow, nice. Debut for that?
Now, I just just want to point out that Max Martin, who wrote "Oops, I did it Again" benefited greatly from the previously great music education system here in Sweden, and it shows in very obvious fashion in this song: it's basically stolen from 400 year old madrigals. 
Richard Thompson included it in his 1000 Years of Popular Music shows a while ago, and it was pretty funny to hear it played in that context.
grand debut for a Friday Adam you knocked it outta the park - bravo! just the right amount of everything tough but doable and the long reveals are delightful.  hope you get to publish more!

I read the clue for MOLERAT and my brain immediately went "mole-asses!" ...never mind that molasses isn't an animal (and doesn't have the e) . I was very amused... and further amused by how close the first thought actually was, when I figured it out.
I would like to posit that naked MOLE RATs live longer than any other rodent due to their complete lack of self consciousness. And they save lots of money not chasing fast fashion!
I liked that a lot. One impenetrable natick, with regard to which I will now head down the epicine rabbit hole.

Finished in a surprisingly quick time, even though I found it relatively tough.

There were plenty of easy down answers to infer the acrosses quite quickly (maybe too many?).

I got caught in the top right corner with epicene and acc. Had to Google why acc was the answer after (I'm not from the USA). Also, in no way being political, I'm really getting quite sick of the profusion of gender-related clues that are appearing in so many crosswords nowadays. If you're going to use scientific terms, at least mix the subject up occasionally...

Thought this was going to be super tough but it was definitely one were things slot so nearly into place once you get a few going. 17 across never looked like a word to me until I was putting in the last couple of letters.
Who else besides me confidently slapped down KOS for [Rocky openings?]?
This is a Wednesday puzzle- not Friday.

EPICENE, wasn't she a character in Les Miz? No? Guess I'm living in my own Private IDAHO. Don't have a Conniption. (A word we don't see often enough.) And when I see Huckleberry I instantly recall Val Kimer as Doc Holliday. A decent Friday. We out.
Fun and easy.

Yo, Adam, I loved your debut puzzle. Great wordplay throughout and nice long entries. Smiles with inlets (small sounds?) and ravioli (hot pockets?). Clever clue for mid. And a reference to Top Chef to boot!

This puzzle made for one astonishing outing.  It brought downhill whoosh as well as uphill labor.  It made me smile.  It gave me fits.  And when it was over, I mused, “Well now, here’s a new constructor that I can’t wait to see more from!”

Look at that gorgeous grid design – never done before in the Times. 

There are only seven longs (answers of eight letters or more), but man, did Adam squeeze the most out of them.  Then, the glory of FEEL GOOD MOVIE and CLOUD NINE abutting the grid's smiley face.  Are you kidding me?

I was misdirected from KOS instead of YOS, to TIE GAME instead of TIE VOTE, to that most glorious [Small sounds] for INLETS.  Happy pings at MAT at the floor of the puzzle and CELLOS on the stage-left of the grid.  And the PuzzPair© of YENTA and [Serious dirt], the clue for another answer.

Bravo, Adam!  I was inspired by your persistence (112 iterations before this final one!) and your talent.  You made all the right decisions on this one.  I loved it. Thank you!
This was a great puzzle, and I hope to see more from this creator. The clues were creative in a way that still made sense, so it was fun to solve.

Fun puzzle. I might not have known Jose MARTI if not for Pete Seeger's introduction to his poem turned into a song Guantanamera. I still remember the time, probably forty years ago, when we got a letter in my office and we were all puzzling about why someone was complaining that a person had been put on a "pedal stool". It made more sense when we figured that one out. I knew 14A instantly despite my nearly complete ignorance of the original singer. Before you dismiss it, though, you should listen to this: https://youtu.be/V4WGsMplGxU?si=xblhdREXId4OEdHD. Everybody who doesn't know Richard Thompson, one of the true musical giants in the world, should get to know his work.
I tell ya what Adam, this was a really good one!

Well I was going to mention the welcoming design but the constructor notes claim it's a smiley face.  Nope, not seeing that.

And that was the highlight. This puzzle is nicely crafted but does not belong on a NYT Friday.  The only thing that gave me any pause (other than yet another sports abbreviation) was the neck flow clue.  Tortured wording but quite fair.  The rest was Tuesdayish.  XWStats users confirm "Easy".  This is on the upper tier though, and I would have been fine with it even pre-Easening.

A good debut that just ran on the wrong day.  (But I understand why; the spanners are intimidating.)

This was a nice, no-lookup Friday. Which I suspect means that the elites will grade it as too easy. I'll take it!

It was amazing how much having ALLOT slowed down my solve though. A very good misdirect.
TIL OOPSIDIDITAGAIN and yOudrivemecrAzy have the same number of letters. And I’m losing my Britney knowledge the older I get.
I have to say, Sam. I truly share your enthusiasm for 13D. Didn’t even register until a few minutes after I finished solving and I smiled a little.
Good stuff!
Well this was a " Good Friday " with both epistolary and apostle in the same puzzle :)

From the "apostle of the Cuban Revolution (Marti) to the apostle referred to as Judas Zelotes in the "Epistle of the Apostles" (was that the first epistolary novel?), this was quite a puzzle, and quite a debut, which I am happy to put on a pedestal.

Some very odd clues today. If you find yourself connipting during an emergency, maybe it would be calming to hold and gently stroke a baby fox. But honestly, I’m as skeptical of that as I am of those who think they can tell your future by looking at your footprints in mashed taro.

Weird. But a fun puzzle anyway.
I see I was posting in my sleep again...

Rainy CT day, and I have to get out and collect the trash bins.
Had YENTe/endOW.
EBOW - that's really a thing?
Deciphering spanners makes me feel smart!
Congratulations on your debut, Adam.
EBOW - wow, haven’t seen  one of those in 40 years
Small sounds was a brilliant clue, loved it. Great puzzle for a Friday.

Impressive Friday puzzle. I just got stuck in a couple of places and couldn't quite work it all out. Appears that I'm alone in that. No big deal. And of course my puzzle find. This was just kind of cute. A Tuesday from July 27, 1999 by Alfio Micci. Some answers in that one: HONEYDEW OVERDUE KATMANDU SCOOBYDOO DERRINGDO Here's that link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=7/27/1999&h=63a Hasta manana. ....

YO. A nicely crunchy Friday, with a couple of gimmes to get me started. EPISTOLARY NOVEL leapt out to this BA (Lit), giving me a helpful anchor to hang a load of crosses on, which in turn gave me Ms Spear’s tune. 
I was confused by SIDE ARM and assumed it was a weapon related thing, but couldn’t match it with clue. As always, it’s been helpfully explained as a sports term here in the comments, so thanks for that.

I have seen all the Rocky films courtesy of the youngest son, so chuckled when I finally filled the Y in. YO.
This was easy for a Friday.
Impossible for me to get EPICENE from crossing ACC, SHEA, and YENTA all in a row. Still don't understand any of those.
Rocky openings made me laugh out loud. What a HOOT.
In re: Sam's column: The term EPICENE is not used in biology. At least I've never seen it, and I am an old biologist.

I loved this one!!  I’ve heard it said that “it was in my wheelhouse” (would love to know where that expression originated) and this one sure was. Having had a baby who screamed for nearly six months with COLIC, that was a given. (He is now 34 so we all got through it!). I’m looking forward to my date night tonight with a FEEL GOOD MOVIE … maybe the crossword documentary?  TGIF folks!  Have a good one.
A fine Friday debut, kudos.
Wow.  Apparently everyone else loved this one.  Personally I thought it was extremely "meh."  Apparently I am alone in that.

Sam,
Re: Tricky Clues
11D. RAVIOLI are stuffed pasta, but they are not noodles.
13D. [Small sounds] is a NYT XWP debut clue for INLETS, but it does follow [Little sounds] from 2021 and [Tiny sound?] for INLET from 2020.

Good morning! Started last night, woke up and had the right perspective immediately on some tricky clues ("Of course it's not a sound-sound, it's a sound!) HAVENOT had this much Friday fun in a while, great debut!
Honestly, a missed opportunity to have “Mail-centric fiction?” not be related to high fantasy or Romantasy. Mail, chain mail? Get it? 😂

FEEL GOOD MOVIE over CLOUD NINE certainly made me feel good.  EPISTOLARY NOVEL always makes me feel good:  Has everyone here read "The Correspondent", I hope?  Wonderful novel and highly recommended if you haven't!  But I must admit I was looking for more of a "mail" pun than EPISTOLARY NOVEL provides and was sort of expecting a knight-in-shining-armor kind of book.

I originally wrote in "TIE game" for the 20-20 clue.  I sure hope there are more VOTEs than that in the mid-terms.  And isn't it interesting that MID and TERMS are in the puzzle.

I found this enjoyable on every level.  Liked the fill and liked the clues.  Easy, yes, but not SO EASY as to be uninteresting.  A nice Friday.

Haven't used the word "epistolary" in a LONG time so that was a fun part of the brain to dust off.  Also loved the "YOs" openings...very cute (and didn't make me suffer eye strain from an overly large roll).  Nice job!
ugh i had DEETS for the longest time. was thinking in legal context, details are crucial.

I think it would be cool to show what percent of the puzzle was completed without assistance. For those of us that do the crossword religiously and sometimes come up short, it would be nice to know, at a glance, how far we got. Just a thought.

As a former boxer, thought I was going to have to be s sourpuss on KOs being Rocky openings (more like closings), so was happily surprised by the clever "Yo"s. 
Thanks for the puzzle!
I got EPISTOLARYNOVEL immediately -- excellent fill/cluing!!

Seemed like a fresh Friday puzzle. Well done!

I finished in 12:23.

This was very fun! I found OOPS I DID IT AGAIN and EPISTOLARY NOVEL pretty quickly and was feeling quite smug about it, but the rest of the puzzle was challenging enough to wipe that smile off my face until I finished. Clever cluing and satisfying long entries throughout - quite an accomplished debut, I’d say!

Wow. I was totally at sea on this one, and yet, not a single time did I think the solution was unfair. I made several small sounds of an ungendered nature while stumbling my way through wrong guess after wrong guess, and even realized I knew the name MARTI. Well done!
Nice! 10/10
I really liked this one! The misdirects added some chew to the solve without making it a slog.
Wow, back-to-back winner puzzles with incremental difficulty and enjoyment! Thanks!

poem made from words in today’s puzzle 



a/ home is made of tea
tea and the mary tyler moore show and d/ any cake left
small sounds of the house
the struggling trees
all the words in the past
a/ our glitter, our good
not all there
not all easy

Not SOEASY, but not too taxing for a Friday. Done without help in about 20 minutes. The lower half seemed easier than the top, and still too many gimmes for a Friday puzzle.

Didn't know EPICENE or EPISTOLARYNOVEL, but knowing the word "epistle" certainly helped me.

Very solid debut puzzle. Congrats!

Not super hard by Friday standards but YENTA/EPICENE is kind of an insane crossing.  Also with ATE CROW hard to spot and EPISTOLARY NOVEL as a crossing.

Big vocab test today.
Enjoyed this one and LOL at "hot pockets" being Ravioli
Buzzed through it until "Rocky openings". Had to be KOs right? Spent ten minutes puzzling over this then suddenly I heard this nasal voice braying "Yo! Adrian!'
Fantastic puzzle today! More like this!

This comments section never fails to disappoint me. 😂 
Lots of compliments for the puzzle. Yet a certain few continue to feel the need to act superior to others. Sad. 

Have a good weekend everyone.

My solve was consistent with the Easy rating in xwstats in that I solved it the same percentage faster as the median solver, although of course my actual solve time was quite a bit slower than those who report there.

However, this easy solve ended up with a couple of mini-puzzles worthy of a Thursday, in my book. Like others I had no idea about the "Not gendered" clue but had EPI_ENE. Figured that had to be a C, but curious how an entire epoch could be non-gendered. Something to look up later.

And then there was that battery powered string player. With K__PAD crossing it, I figured it was easier to focus on Rocky. I mentally sounded out letters for him, pausing at kOS and progressing onward until, when I got to Y, I could hear Stallone's voice. At that point it no longer mattered that I knew naught of the string player. Something else to look up later.
Smooth start but a Rocky finish and had to look up in the SW corner.  Fun one though.   Many thanks.

St Paul's letters to the Corinthians, Ephesians, et al, were Epistles, so 17A wasn't too much of a stretch for me. Still, a new word for the bank. Also, how many doors there are in the White House. But they keep remodeling everything, so who knows for sure?

Hated EPISTOLARYNOVEL… and it had some rather difficult crosses. The rest was surprisingly relatively easy for me. 

But….. Anytime I can complete a Friday without lookups I always feel like….

Yo Adrian!!!! I did it!!!! 

Rating:
8:10

For anyone who doesn't get the Gameplay emails or check the full Gameplay feed with any regularity (guilty), here's a link to a post that contains a link to a bonus puzzle co-contsructed by Rian Johnson and our Christina. I think the post calls it a Tuesday difficulty solve, and I'd have to agree with that. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/crosswords/special-detective-novel-crossword-puzzle.html?unlocked_article_code=1.JFE.HjFh.ih5cx6DdqnHA&smid=url-share
This was the rare week when I enjoyed Friday’s puzzle much more than Thursday’s. Thanks for the smile, Adam.

Fun puzzle. I thought I was going to sail right through but needed a few lookups.

I tried to identify the quartet in the Wordplay photo without success. The internet in Visual Search sometimes refers to this as a barbershop quartet but that looks like no barbershop quartet to me--more like The Three Tenors. Anyone know who they are? "Jason Davis/Getty Images" are credited.

Any suggestion for a FEELGOODMOVIE? I'm watching a biopic on the history of the Eagles on Netflix now.

Fun one!

Struggled with EPISTOLARY and EPICENE, but worked out it with the crossings.
Welcome Adam Shapiro. Fun puzzle, good clues.
17 across reminded me of the absolute torture of reading "Clarissa" for a college English class.

What a treat! I got the gold star after mucking around in the SW corner for a short eternity trying to clear up KEYPAD, EBOW, and YOS.

I just happened to look up the major conferences last week so ACC was a gimme, but I would've been running the alphabet otherwise trying to cross with EPICENE, which I've never heard of. EPISTOLARY NOVEL was pretty unreal and I can't believe I got it.

Loved this one! Tough but fair.

The special crossword is titled "Whodunnit?"

It is not surprising that this constructor has used the spelling that is not the preferred one in the New York Times. That would be "Whodunit".

(Also, the PBS show NOVA is about many things other than the cosmos.)
I believe the Epicene was between the Pliocene and Miocene Epochs. I'll have to look it up.
I did well on the bottom two thirds, but the top third did me in. I learned two cool words though (epicene and epistolary) so it's all good.
This was fun and the clues were great! Loved it!
Another excellent debut...bravo!!

Bravo, Adam Shapiro! Great puzzle! I especially adored CLOUD NINE smack in the center of the grid. As I commented somewhere below, my introduction as a teenager to the EPISTOLARY NOVEL is still a fave of the genre for me — and appropriately trans-Atlantic, NYC to London: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/84%2C_Charing_Cross_Road Wordplay community, if you haven't read Adam's notes over at XWord Info, they are an excellent exploration of what it took for him to get this puzzle to press. Again, congratulations on a wonderful grid. Your perseverance glows! https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=10/16/2026

14a made my Elder Millennial heart so happy (and I knew it immediately without any crosses 😂). 
Congrats on a fine debut! I loved it!
Stuck way too long on ALLOT/KAPOT, which I assumed must have been from the Krazy Kat era. I see now how that W makes much more sense.

I saw that EBOW might be a fill knowing what one was but discounted the likelihood of it being correct thinking that it was probably too obscure. I know professional musicians who don't know what they are. 

I guess more people know of them than I thought. I was sure it was an electronatick.

@Hector Pefo
I'm in agreement about the long entries.  At 58 years old, I've heard of 14A, but I was not going to get it from just the lyrics.  17A is a phrase I'm aware of, but maybe it's just obscure enough for a Friday.

@Selective Walrus for some reason, I found the bottom half closer to a Wednesday, but the top half was a proper Friday for me.

Seriously, the word you're probably talking about isn't a political term.  Its most common meaning is "indistinguishable in form by gender,"  such as an animal that you'd have to get far too close to for comfort in order to tell what gender it is, which is most animals, but not, say, a lion, the male of which can be distinguished by his mane, or people, where the two genders have distinguishably different shapes, which is why bathroom pictograms exist for the two genders.

Other definitions include "having the characteristics of the opposite gender" and "lacking the characteristics of either gender."

It also can have a grammatical meaning in many languages; for example, in French, "élève espiègle" can mean "mischievous schoolboy" or "schoolgirl," but the article chosen (un/une) can distinguish which is meant, or (l') leave it ambiguous.

But this is not a hot-button political word.

@Liz Evans The figurative meaning of "in my wheelhouse" is from baseball. It describes the part of the strike zone (or even slightly outside it) where any given batter can hit the ball with the most power and precision. One site describes the transition from literal to figurative wheelhouse thusly: Think of the Mickey Mouse cartoon Steamboat Willie, where Mickey is steering the boat. Baseball announcers in the mid-twentieth century saw the bat swing as somewhat like a wheel, and when a batter could really tee off on a ball pitched in a certain location, the announcer said the pitch was right in his wheelhouse. So in a matter of a short time, we go from Mickey Mouse to Mickey Mantle. The meaning migrated farther, from baseball to analogous things in real life, in the 1980s. Thus: “Acting roles that also include boxing are in Mickey Rourke’s wheelhouse.” https://www.writerscentre.com.au/blog/qa-the-origin-of-in-your-wheelhouse/
To be clear, the literal meaning of "in my wheelhouse" is from a ship's wheelhouse.
